cues.text: A Reluctant Heir
Born in 1556 at the castle of Calasanza in Aragon, Spain, Joseph was the youngest of five children of a noble family.
After his mother and brother died, his father pressed him to marry and continue the family line.
A severe illness brought Joseph to the point of death and convinced him instead to pursue the priesthood.
He was ordained in 1583 after completing rigorous studies in law and theology.
Confronting Neglected Children in Rome
Settling in Rome in 1592, Joseph joined the Confraternity of Christian Doctrine and was struck by the enormous number of poor and orphaned children.
They roamed the city's streets, many having lost parents to plague or poverty, with no access to any education at all.
He began personally gathering these children and bringing them to whatever schooling could be arranged.
The First Free Public School in Europe
When the paid teachers Joseph relied on refused to take on additional unpaid students, the pastor of Santa Dorotea’s church offered him two rooms and his own assistance.
Joined by two more priests, Joseph opened, in November 1597, what historians recognize as the first free public school in Europe , open to any child regardless of family means.
Pope Clement VIII provided an annual subsidy, and within a short time roughly a thousand children were under Joseph's care.
Founding the Piarists
In 1602, Joseph gathered his growing circle of assistant teachers into formal community life.
This laid the foundation of what became the Piarists (Clerics Regular of the Pious Schools).
Their members took a distinctive fourth vow specifically dedicated to educating youth, especially the poor.
Pope Paul V formally recognized the congregation in 1617.
Suspicion, Opposition, and a Friendship with Galileo
The idea of educating poor children for free struck many contemporaries as dangerously radical.
They believed educated poor people would refuse to remain in their traditional labor.
Joseph faced sustained opposition from outside critics and, eventually, internal dissension within his rapidly growing order.
His friendship with the astronomer Galileo Galilei drew further suspicion during the tense years of the Galileo controversy.
Several young Piarists studied under the great scientist.
For a period, Joseph was even removed from leadership of his own institute before being restored before his death.
Legacy
Joseph died in Rome in 1648, having lived to see his order grow to some 500 members across six provinces.
Canonized in 1767, he is remembered as the founder of popular Catholic education for the poor.
Piarist schools carry forward this legacy, continuing to operate on five continents.
He is honored today as the patron saint of Catholic schools generally.
